summary: Defines a new SIP response code that tells a caller their call was rejected because it was anonymous. This lets the caller retry without hiding their identity. It is on the standards track.

eli5.summary: If you call someone with your number hidden and they refuse, this tells you why. You can then try again with your name showing.

questions: how to reject anonymous sip calls
what does sip response code 433 mean
can a caller retry after a 433
subtitle: A SIP response code that says a call was refused because the caller hid their identity.

tldr.problem: SIP lets users call anonymously, and callees may refuse anonymous calls, but the only close response code, 403 (Forbidden), gives no machine-readable reason.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines the 433 (Anonymity Disallowed) response code, lists when a request counts as anonymous, and says a caller must get the user's consent before retrying without anonymity.
tldr.outcome: Callers and gateways can now handle an anonymity rejection programmatically, though the RFC warns the code is likely ineffective against SIP-based spam.

today: RFC 5079 is a Proposed Standard from December 2007, and no obsoleting or updating RFC is listed for it.

sections.title: The Problem with Rejecting Anonymous Calls
sections.content:
SIP lets users place anonymous calls. In RFC 3261 this is done with a From header field whose display name is "Anonymous". RFC 3323 added the Privacy header field for greater levels of anonymity, and RFC 3325 added the P-Asserted-Identity header field.

People who receive such calls keep the right to reject them for being anonymous. The closest existing response is 403 (Forbidden), which gives no specific reason. A reason phrase can say so to a human, but it is no use to software and cannot be read by a caller who speaks another language.

A code that software can understand allows programmatic handling, such as user interface prompts, or conversion to equivalent error codes in the PSTN when the client is a gateway. RFC 5079 defines the 433 (Anonymity Disallowed) response code for this.
sections.eli5: Saying "no" to a hidden caller used to be like a locked door with no sign. 433 puts up a sign that even a robot can read: "we do not take calls from people who hide who they are."

sections.title: When a Server Sends 433
sections.content:
A server, usually acting for the called party, MAY send 433 when it gets an anonymous request and refuses it because the requestor is anonymous. A request SHOULD be treated as anonymous when the originator has explicitly withheld its identity. The RFC lists four cases:

  • The From header field has a URI in the anonymous.invalid domain.
  • The From display name is Anonymous or anonymous. The RFC admits this is a weak signal, because display names are meant for humans and language variations or misspellings can fool software, but RFC 3261 names it as a way to declare anonymity.
  • The request has a Privacy header field with the value id or user.
  • The From URI carries an explicit indication of anonymity. This holds even if the request has a validated Identity header field from RFC 4474.
sections.eli5: The server looks for clues that the caller hid on purpose, like a name that says "Anonymous" or a request to keep the identity secret. Only then does it use 433.

sections.title: What Does Not Count as Anonymous
sections.content:
Some cases look anonymous but are not, and the RFC says 433 should not be used for them. A missing network-asserted identity, such as no P-Asserted-Identity, SHOULD NOT by itself be treated as anonymity. A Privacy value of id removes that header, but a server cannot tell this apart from an origin domain that never supported it. Such a request is anonymous only if there is another sign, such as a display name of Anonymous.

Likewise, a request whose identity cannot be determined or validated, but not because of anything the requestor did, is not anonymous. For example, a request with a normal From and Identity and Identity-Info header fields whose certificate cannot be fetched is not anonymous, and 433 SHOULD NOT be used.
sections.eli5: If the caller did not hide anything and the problem is just a broken check on our side, that is not hiding. Only on-purpose hiding counts.

sections.title: What the Caller Does Next
sections.content:
A User Agent Client (UAC) that receives 433 MUST NOT retry the request without anonymity unless the user confirms this is wanted. The confirmation could come from the user interface or from user-defined policy. If the user agrees, the UAC MAY retry without requesting anonymity.

The reason is that silently retrying would break the user's expectations: the user might think the call was made anonymously when it was not.

A 433 to a mid-dialog request SHOULD NOT end the dialog or the specific usage of that dialog (RFC 5057). A UAC that does not understand 433 treats it as a 400 response.
sections.eli5: If the door says no, you must ask the person who wanted to stay hidden before trying again with your name showing. A computer must not unmask you on its own.

sections.title: The 433 Definition and Registration
sections.content:
The definition is short: the 433 response indicates that the server refused to fulfill the request because the requestor was anonymous. Its default reason phrase is "Anonymity Disallowed".

Section 6 registers the code in the SIP response code registry under the procedures of RFC 3261, giving RFC Number RFC 5079, Response Code Number 433 and Default Reason Phrase "Anonymity Disallowed".
sections.eli5: The RFC gives the new answer a number, 433, and a name, "Anonymity Disallowed", and writes them in the official list.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Sending 433 reveals that the called party does not accept anonymous calls. If that is sensitive, a UAS SHOULD reject with 403 instead.

In the PSTN, Anonymous Call Rejection is commonly used against telemarketers, who often withhold their identity. The RFC says 433 is likely ineffective against SIP-based spam, because a malicious caller can send a non-anonymous but meaningless and invalid From and display name. Without a Privacy header field, that request will not appear anonymous and will not be blocked.

If an anonymizer acting as a RFC 3323 back-to-back user agent gets a 433, it MUST NOT retry without anonymization unless the user explicitly configured it to do so.
sections.eli5: Saying "I do not take hidden calls" tells the caller something about you. And a sneaky caller can just use a fake name instead of hiding, so this does not stop junk calls.
